situation: You are asking why winters in places like Britain, Ireland and Norway are far milder than in parts of Canada at about the same latitude. Reported fact: the contrast is real and large. The open question is which causes do the most work: warm ocean currents, prevailing winds, the sea's ability to store heat, or the shape and mountains of the continents. Your goal seems to be understanding, so the useful result is a clearer picture of the competing explanations and a sharper next question.

minds.title: The Ocean Cartographer
minds.concern: Rivers of warm water in the sea, charted as real, nameable currents that carry heat to particular coasts.
minds.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
minds.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea

minds.title: The Conveyor Theorist
minds.concern: The whole ocean as one connected circulation, where heat delivered to the north Atlantic depends on deep sinking and return flow, and can change.
minds.author: Wallace S. Broecker

minds.title: The Atmosphere Physicist
minds.concern: Air, not water, as the main carrier of heat, with winds, land and sea differences, and energy budgets deciding who gets a mild winter.
minds.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert

debate.speaker: The Ocean Cartographer
debate.text: Start with the obvious answer: the Gulf Stream. A great warm river leaves the tropics and washes the shores of western Europe. Draw the currents on a map and the mild coasts line up with them. Why look further than the thing you can literally chart?
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Because a map shows where water goes, not where winter warmth comes from. Winter air over Europe arrives on the westerly winds, and those winds cross the Atlantic whatever the currents do. The question is how much heat the ocean hands to that air, and whether the current is the main supplier.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Theorist
debate.text: I would defend the ocean without claiming it works alone. The Atlantic carries a lot of heat northward, and it only keeps doing so because cold water sinks in the far north and pulls more warm water in behind it. Remove that pull and the heat delivery weakens. Your map shows a river, but it hides an engine.
debate.author: Wallace S. Broecker
debate.basis: Basis: Wallace S. Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Fair, the engine matters. But test it against Canada: the Pacific coast of British Columbia is also mild in winter, and no Gulf Stream goes there. Winds off a warm-ish ocean can do the job on their own. So a current is sufficient to explain some of Europe, but maybe not necessary.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Ocean Cartographer
debate.text: I concede the Pacific coast is a good counterexample to my first answer. But note what it proves: the sea is the common factor. Where westerly air has crossed open water first, winters are gentle. Where it has crossed a continent, they are brutal. Water is doing the work, whether by current or by sheer presence.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Agreed, and here is the physical reason, which goes beyond what Maury offered. Water takes a lot of heat to warm and gives much of it back slowly. The ocean banks summer warmth and releases it in winter, while land loses it fast. Europe sits downwind of that bank. Eastern Canada sits downwind of a cold continent.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Theorist
debate.text: Heat storage explains the mildness of any coast, though. It does not explain why Europe beats Newfoundland, both being ocean-facing. The cold Labrador side and the warm Norwegian side differ because of different water arriving. That difference is the conveyor, and you cannot bank heat that never arrived.
debate.author: Wallace S. Broecker
debate.basis: Basis: Wallace S. Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Partly yes. Surface water east and west of the Atlantic does differ, and that matters locally. But there is another suspect neither of you has named: big mountain ranges like the Rockies bend the westerly winds into a pattern that sends cold air south over eastern North America and warm air north over Europe. That is my own extension, not a claim from my source.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Ocean Cartographer
debate.text: Then my chart is incomplete, not wrong. Currents still move real heat, but if mountains steer the wind, a draw of warm water on a map overstates my case. I would now claim only that the sea is necessary and the current is one contributor whose share is argued over.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Theorist
debate.text: I will narrow mine too. If winds and heat storage supply much of the baseline, then the conveyor is less about why Europe is mild today and more about how fragile or stable that mildness might be over long timescales. Still, I would not let anyone call the ocean circulation a footnote. How big its share is remains genuinely disputed.
debate.author: Wallace S. Broecker
debate.basis: Basis: Wallace S. Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor

clearer: The main insight is that there is probably no single cause. The sea matters in at least two ways: it stores summer heat and releases it in winter, and ocean circulation delivers warm water northward. Prevailing westerly winds carry that maritime influence onto land, and large mountain ranges may shape which continent gets cold or warm air. What remains disputed is the relative share of the currents versus the winds and mountains. A possible self-reflection: when you hear a one-word answer like the Gulf Stream, you might ask whether it explains the difference or only names one ingredient.
dependsOn: Competing explanations and what would separate them: (1) If ocean currents are the dominant cause, then regions with a similar current but different winds should still be mild, and mildness should track the strength of northward ocean heat transport. (2) If heat storage plus westerly winds dominate, then any coast downwind of open ocean should be mild, as the Pacific coast of Canada suggests, with or without a Gulf Stream. (3) If mountains and large-scale wind patterns matter most, then climate models with the Rockies removed or flattened should show much colder Europe or milder eastern North America. A proportionate way to learn more: compare winter temperatures along the same latitude at coastal and inland sites on both sides of the Atlantic and Pacific, and look up published model experiments that switch off one factor at a time.
